paragraphs: The paper asks how good graph neural networks can theoretically be at finding approximate solutions to combinatorial problems. An approximation ratio describes how a solution compares with the best possible one. This shifts attention from whether a network performs well on examples to what quality of solution its architecture can support.

The authors introduce a class of graph neural networks that can solve a strictly broader collection of problems than existing architectures. They then connect these networks to distributed local algorithms. That connection supplies tools for establishing achievable approximation ratios for minimum dominating set and minimum vertex cover, along with limits that apply to widely used architectures such as GIN, GAT, GCN, and GraphSAGE.

A further result shows that supplying node coloring or weak-coloring information improves the approximation ratios. Consequently, the capabilities being analyzed depend on both the network and its input features. The contribution gives a theoretical reason for preprocessing: appropriately structured node information can strengthen the solution guarantees available to a graph neural network.
neurips-2019-approximation-ratios-of-gra.tldr: The paper establishes approximation guarantees and limits for graph neural networks and proves that node-coloring features can improve those guarantees.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether guarantees comparing shallow residual networks with linear predictors extend to networks with multiple residual blocks. It first gives examples showing both the promise and difficulty of that extension. A ResNet can have strictly better local minima than a fully connected ReLU network on some datasets, yet successive residual blocks need not produce monotonically improving representations, even at a global optimum.

The main theorem establishes a conditional guarantee for deep ResNets. Under specified geometric conditions, every critical point either performs at least as well as the best linear predictor or has a Hessian with a strictly negative eigenvalue. The latter identifies a direction of negative curvature, distinguishing such a point from an ordinary local minimum.

The result explains how a chain of skip connections can improve the optimization landscape. It does not assert that every deep ResNet strictly outperforms linear prediction. The authors also analyze regions where residual transformations are near the identity, obtaining depth-independent upper bounds on critical-point risk and Rademacher complexity.
neurips-2019-are-deep-resnets-provably-b.tldr: Under geometric conditions, deep ResNet critical points either match the best linear predictor or possess a direction of negative curvature.

paragraphs: In a multi-armed bandit experiment, the observations collected from an option can influence subsequent decisions about the experiment. Its sample average therefore need not be an unbiased estimate of its true average reward. The paper separates three places where this dependence arises: choosing which arm to sample, deciding when to stop, and choosing which arm's estimate to examine.

The authors introduce a mathematical notion of optimism that captures particular monotonic behaviors in these decisions. Under the corresponding optimistic rules, the sources of bias point in different directions. Adaptive sampling induces negative bias, while adaptive stopping and adaptive selection of an arm induce positive bias. These conclusions concern the defined rule classes, rather than every possible adaptive procedure.

The analysis uses a general stochastic bandit setting and does not depend on whether the experiment aims to minimize regret or identify the best arm. Examples illustrate each rule type, and simulations support the predicted bias directions. The practical lesson is that interpreting an estimate requires distinguishing how observations, stopping, and final selection were determined.
neurips-2019-are-sample-means-in-multi-a.tldr: For defined optimistic bandit rules, adaptive sampling biases sample means downward, while adaptive stopping and arm selection bias them upward.

paragraphs: E2-Train addresses the energy required to train convolutional networks, motivated by the possibility of training directly on devices with limited resources. Its central idea is to reduce the computations performed during learning. The paper combines changes at three levels so that savings can come from data processing, model updates, and the arithmetic used in back-propagation.

At the data level, it stochastically drops mini-batches. At the model level, it selectively updates layers. At the algorithm level, it uses sign prediction to support lower-cost, lower-precision back-propagation. These strategies target different parts of training, and the authors examine their contributions through simulations and ablation studies, supported by actual energy measurements from an FPGA board.

The reported tradeoffs depend on the training setting. For ResNet-74 on CIFAR-10, energy reductions above 90% and 60% accompany top-1 accuracy losses of about 2% and 1.2%, respectively. For ResNet-110 on CIFAR-100, savings exceed 84% without reduced inference accuracy. These examples demonstrate substantial measured savings, including both accuracy-preserving and accuracy-trading configurations.
neurips-2019-e2-train-training-state-of-.tldr: E2-Train reduces CNN training energy through batch dropping, selective layer updates, and cheaper back-propagation, with substantial savings in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Neural interfaces that stimulate cells need calibration to determine how electrical inputs produce neural responses. As electrode counts increase, collecting enough measurements becomes difficult. This paper studies whether information from earlier experiments and measurements chosen during calibration can reduce that burden, using electrical recording and stimulation in primate retina as a laboratory prototype for an artificial retina.

The authors improve three calibration components. For spike sorting, similarities in electrical stimulation artifacts across electrodes and experiments reduce the measurements needed. For response modeling, a joint model uses a relationship observed in previous retinas: larger recorded spike amplitudes correspond to lower stimulation thresholds. For adaptive stimulation, probability estimates from existing measurements guide which electrodes to stimulate next.

Both sharing information across cells and choosing measurements adaptively improve efficiency. Similar gains arise from non-adaptive stimulation with a joint model and adaptive stimulation with separate models for individual cells. Image reconstruction results suggest that more efficient calibration may improve artificial-retina performance, while keeping that potential application distinct from the demonstrated laboratory calibration improvements.
neurips-2019-efficient-characterization-.tldr: Prior experimental information and adaptive stimulation make retinal-interface calibration more efficient, with reconstruction results suggesting potential artificial-retina benefits.

paragraphs: The paper adapts Transformers for time-series forecasting by addressing two weaknesses identified in the standard architecture. Pointwise attention can overlook local context, making forecasts vulnerable to anomalous observations. Meanwhile, attention memory grows quadratically with sequence length, restricting how much history a model can directly process when memory is limited.

To incorporate nearby observations into attention, the authors generate queries and keys using causal convolutions. Attention comparisons can then reflect local patterns instead of relying only on individual time points. They also introduce LogSparse Transformer, whose memory requirement grows as O(L(log L)^2) for sequence length L. This substantially changes how memory requirements increase as longer histories are considered.

The two changes address complementary forecasting needs: recognizing local context and retaining access to long-term information. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets compare favorably with the state of the art. The abstract specifically reports improved forecasting for finely sampled series with strong long-term dependencies under constrained memory, connecting the architectural changes to a setting where both weaknesses matter.
neurips-2019-enhancing-the-locality-and-.tldr: Convolutional attention and a sparse Transformer design improve local-context modeling and reduce memory requirements for long time-series forecasting.

paragraphs: Markov chain Monte Carlo uses proposed moves to explore a target probability distribution that is difficult to handle directly. Its effectiveness depends on the proposal distribution, which determines the candidate moves. This paper introduces a gradient-based method for learning that distribution automatically, reducing reliance on a well-chosen proposal at the start.

The authors define an entropy-regularized objective called a generalized speed measure and optimize proposal parameters using stochastic gradients. A central feature is that learning continues even when a proposed state is rejected. Rejection therefore does not prevent the adaptation mechanism from updating the proposal. This matters especially in early iterations, when a poor initial proposal may make successful moves difficult.

The framework is applied to multivariate random-walk Metropolis and Metropolis-adjusted Langevin proposals, including full covariance matrices that describe relationships among movement directions. Experiments provide evidence that the method can outperform other MCMC algorithms, including Hamiltonian Monte Carlo schemes. The stated finding is empirical and establishes potential advantages of the adaptation strategy rather than a universal ranking of samplers.
neurips-2019-gradient-based-adaptive-mar.tldr: A gradient-based MCMC adaptation method learns proposal distributions even from rejected moves and empirically can outperform other samplers.

paragraphs: Graph kernels and graph neural networks offer different strengths for learning from graphs. Kernels are relatively straightforward to train and support theoretical guarantees, but handcrafted graph features can restrict their expressive power. Graph neural networks extract more complex information through multiple nonlinear layers, while introducing difficult optimization and many hyperparameters.

The paper constructs Graph Neural Tangent Kernels, which correspond to infinitely wide multilayer graph neural networks trained by gradient descent. This correspondence brings the graph-processing capabilities of those networks into a kernel formulation. The approach aims to retain neural-network expressiveness while obtaining the training and analytical advantages associated with graph kernels, connecting two methods that otherwise appear quite different.

The authors prove that these kernels can learn a class of smooth functions on graphs. They also report strong empirical results on graph classification datasets. The theoretical and experimental findings address separate questions: the proof establishes learnability for a particular function class, while the classification results demonstrate practical performance on the tested datasets.
neurips-2019-graph-neural-tangent-kernel.tldr: Graph Neural Tangent Kernels connect infinitely wide graph neural networks with kernel learning, yielding learnability guarantees and strong graph-classification results.

paragraphs: Using fewer bits for numerical values can make neural-network computation more efficient, but the representation must preserve information needed for learning. Earlier eight-bit floating-point training worked for selected models yet substantially degraded networks such as MobileNet and Transformer. This paper attributes that difficulty to different precision requirements in the forward and backward passes.

The authors propose a hybrid eight-bit floating-point format, HFP8, together with an end-to-end distributed training procedure. The hybrid approach addresses the differing numerical demands within training. They demonstrate training across image classification, object detection, language, and speech applications without accuracy degradation in the reported evaluations, broadening the demonstrated applicability of eight-bit training.

The paper also studies deployment of already trained models. It reports that models can be converted to the new eight-bit format without losing accuracy by fine-tuning batch-normalization statistics. Together, the training and conversion results support the use of the proposed format in hardware for both building and deploying neural networks, rather than limiting its role to one phase.
neurips-2019-hybrid-8-bit-floating-point.tldr: A hybrid eight-bit floating-point format supports training and model conversion without accuracy loss in the paper's reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Evaluating generated images requires a way to measure how realistic they appear to people. Automated scores provide indirect signals, while informal human evaluations can be hard to compare or reproduce. HYPE develops a standardized human benchmark grounded in research on visual perception, with attention to reliability, distinguishing models, and evaluation cost.

The benchmark has two variants. One adjusts viewing time to identify a perceptual threshold associated with generated outputs appearing real. The other removes time constraints and measures how often people misclassify real and generated images. The second variant is less expensive, giving the benchmark two ways to assess realism with different time and cost requirements.

The authors evaluate six generative adversarial networks and two sampling techniques across conditional and unconditional generation using four image datasets. HYPE tracks improvements over training epochs, and bootstrap analysis supports the consistency and reproducibility of its model rankings. These findings show that a structured human evaluation procedure can provide repeatable comparisons of perceived realism across the tested models.
neurips-2019-hype-a-benchmark-for-human-.tldr: HYPE standardizes human judgments of generated-image realism and demonstrates reproducible model rankings using timed and untimed evaluations.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization searches for useful hyperparameter settings by evaluating a training objective and using those results to guide subsequent choices. Even when related tasks have already been solved, the search may still spend effort exploring initially. This paper proposes transferring information from earlier tasks through learned representations of their training datasets.

The method represents datasets using distribution embeddings in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. These representations describe a task through its data distribution and enter a joint Gaussian process model alongside hyperparameters. The model can therefore relate objective behavior to both the chosen settings and the dataset on which those settings are used. Dataset information becomes part of the mechanism for transferring experience.

The authors report faster convergence than existing baselines, with some cases needing only a few evaluations of the target objective. That qualification matters: the abstract does not claim that every new task needs so few evaluations. The result supports using distributional descriptions of datasets to make prior optimization experience useful when tuning a target task.
neurips-2019-hyperparameter-learning-via.tldr: Learning representations of dataset distributions lets Bayesian optimization transfer across tasks and converge faster in reported comparisons.

paragraphs: Tasks that reward an agent only when it reaches a goal can be difficult to learn because successful behavior provides infrequent feedback. Rewarding progress according to distance from the goal gives more guidance, but it can also create local optima where learning settles without solving the task. This paper addresses that failure of straightforward distance-based rewards.

The proposed model-free method adds an auxiliary distance-based reward constructed from pairs of rollouts. This extra comparison encourages diverse exploration and prevents learning from stabilizing around the local optima induced by naive shaping in the studied tasks. The augmented objective also approaches the original sparse-reward objective as the agent learns to succeed, aligning the eventual training signal with task completion.

The authors report success on difficult exploration problems, including maze navigation and three-dimensional construction in Minecraft. In those evaluations, naive distance shaping fails, while intrinsic-curiosity and reward-relabeling strategies perform poorly. The contribution is a way to make distance guidance more effective without additional task-specific reward engineering or domain expertise.
neurips-2019-keeping-your-distance-solvi.tldr: An auxiliary reward comparing pairs of rollouts improves exploration and helps distance-shaped learning solve difficult sparse-reward goal tasks.

paragraphs: This paper studies what overparameterized neural networks can provably learn and why having many parameters need not force excessive sample requirements. Its guarantees cover particular concept classes, including functions represented by smaller two- and three-layer networks with smooth activations. The result concerns identifiable families of learnable functions rather than every possible prediction problem.

The authors prove that stochastic gradient descent or its variants can learn these classes in polynomial time using polynomially many samples. They also show that sample complexity can be almost independent of the number of parameters in the learning network. This separates the size of the model used for optimization from the amount of data needed for the stated learning guarantees.

The analysis goes beyond the linear approximation associated with neural tangent kernel arguments. It introduces a quadratic approximation of the network and connects that approximation with theory about stochastic gradient descent escaping saddle points. This additional structure provides a route to learning and generalization guarantees that extend beyond the earlier linearized treatment.
neurips-2019-learning-and-generalization.tldr: A quadratic network analysis proves efficient learning of specified function classes with sample requirements almost independent of the overparameterized model's size.

paragraphs: Training can improve when examples are weighted differently or when additional examples are created through augmentation. These interventions are often designed and learned using separate methods. This paper proposes a shared gradient-based approach that learns different data-manipulation strategies while also training the model that uses the resulting data.

The method builds on a connection between supervised learning and reinforcement learning. It adapts an existing reward-learning algorithm, with a parameterized data-reward function determining which manipulation scheme is obtained. Changing that parameterization allows the same learning framework to express different interventions. The paper demonstrates augmentation through a learned text-transformation network and weighting through dynamically changing the importance of training samples.

Experiments report significant improvements in image and text classification in settings with little training data or imbalanced classes. These results support both the usefulness of the demonstrated manipulation schemes and the broader idea of learning them through a common objective. The central contribution is the shared learning mechanism, rather than a separate handcrafted procedure for each type of data manipulation.
neurips-2019-learning-data-manipulation-.tldr: A shared gradient-based framework jointly learns data augmentation or sample weighting and improves classification in low-data and class-imbalanced experiments.

paragraphs: The paper studies visual reasoning through Raven's Progressive Matrices, a task used here to investigate reasoning about relationships in visual inputs. Its motivation is that strong performance on specialized AI tasks does not automatically establish the ability to reason spatially and temporally. The authors focus on improving this particular form of perceptual inference.

Their Contrastive Perceptual Inference network, CoPINet, draws on contrast effects discussed in psychology, cognition, and education. They use this idea to design and train a permutation-invariant model, so the modeled collection is not treated differently merely because its elements are reordered. A simple inference module is trained jointly with the perception backbone, connecting visual processing with the reasoning component.

CoPINet achieves the reported best performance among permutation-invariant models on two major datasets. The authors interpret their results as supporting reasoning from pixels by considering possibilities consistent with relationships among objects. The empirical achievement is specifically within the evaluated visual-reasoning tasks and model category; its significance is the demonstrated combination of perception, contrast, and jointly learned inference.
neurips-2019-learning-perceptual-inferen.tldr: CoPINet combines contrast-inspired learning with joint perception and inference, achieving leading results among permutation-invariant models on two visual-reasoning datasets.

paragraphs: The Levenshtein Transformer treats sequence generation as a process of inserting and deleting tokens. These operations let it construct a sequence or revise one that already exists, while changing its length along the way. This addresses the rigidity of methods that generate strictly step by step or repeatedly modify a sequence whose length is bounded.

The model is partially autoregressive, and its training procedures use the complementary nature of insertion and deletion. One operation supplies learning signals for the other. Bringing both operations into a single model connects generation and refinement: adding missing material and removing unwanted material become parts of the same sequence-processing approach.

Experiments cover generation tasks such as translation and summarization, along with refinement through automatic post-editing. The authors report comparable or better performance with substantially improved efficiency in these evaluations. They also show that a model trained for machine translation can be used directly for automatic post-editing, providing evidence that the editing-based formulation supports flexibility across the two uses.
neurips-2019-levenshtein-transformer-51d.tldr: The Levenshtein Transformer generates and refines variable-length sequences through learned insertion and deletion, improving efficiency in reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Many learning-theory guarantees assume that training examples are independently and identically distributed. This paper instead considers examples whose dependencies are described by a graph. Its aim is to understand generalization in that setting while accounting for the behavior of the learning algorithm, rather than relying on an independence assumption that the data do not satisfy.

The authors establish McDiarmid-type concentration inequalities for Lipschitz functions of graph-dependent random variables. Such inequalities control how far a function of random data can deviate from its expected value. Their bounds depend on a graph quantity called forest complexity, which measures the strength of the dependency structure. They show that this quantity is small for many forms of dependent data, allowing useful concentration.

The new inequalities then support stability-based generalization bounds. Stability relates the sensitivity of a learning algorithm to changes in its data to its ability to generalize. The contribution therefore connects dependency structure, concentration, and algorithm behavior, providing a route to guarantees when examples are related rather than independent.
neurips-2019-mcdiarmid-type-inequalities.tldr: New concentration inequalities use graph forest complexity to derive stability-based generalization bounds for learning from dependent examples.

paragraphs: Data about related quantities are often reported at different scales, such as averages over different regions or time periods. Those differences complicate learning the quantities together because their observations describe different aggregations. This paper develops a Gaussian process model that explicitly includes the aggregation scale of each task in a shared statistical representation.

Each task combines latent processes that are integrated at its own scale. Sharing these underlying processes connects tasks, while task-specific integration represents how their measurements were collected. The authors derive ways to calculate cross-covariances between tasks analytically or numerically. These covariances express how observations remain related even when they summarize different spatial or temporal scales.

The framework also permits different likelihood models for different tasks. A variational lower bound can be optimized stochastically, making the approach suitable for larger datasets. Demonstrations include synthetic data, fertility data, and air-pollution prediction. Together, these examples illustrate a modeling approach that incorporates aggregation into joint learning instead of requiring all observations to share one input scale.
neurips-2019-multi-task-learning-for-agg.tldr: A multi-task Gaussian process model jointly learns related quantities observed at different aggregation scales using shared, integrated latent processes.

paragraphs: The paper studies sequential forecasting when the underlying sequence has bounded total variation, meaning its accumulated changes are limited. Observations contain independent subgaussian noise. The challenge is to predict as data arrive while adapting to how much the sequence changes, even when that variation budget is unknown.

The proposed algorithm runs in O(n log n) time. With high probability, its cumulative squared error is bounded, up to logarithmic factors, by n^(1/3) C_n^(2/3) sigma^(4/3) + C_n^2, where C_n bounds variation and sigma describes noise. A matching lower bound establishes optimal dependence on these parameters up to a logarithmic factor. The method uses the localized structure of Haar wavelets and adaptation ideas from wavelet smoothing.

The authors also identify a barrier for linear forecasters, a class including online gradient descent variants with fixed restart schedules. These methods require a worse square-root dependence on sequence length in the stated regret comparison. This explains why more adaptive forecasting is necessary to attain the optimal rate in this setting.
neurips-2019-online-forecasting-of-total.tldr: A fast wavelet-based forecaster adapts to unknown total variation and achieves an error bound matching the lower bound up to logarithmic factors.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning that protects information about its reward function. The privacy objective makes neighboring reward functions indistinguishable under differential privacy, helping prevent reward information from being recovered through methods such as inverse reinforcement learning. Continuous state spaces create a difficulty for existing approaches because their required noise can grow without bound as the state space becomes infinite.

The proposed method adds functional noise to the value-function approximator repeatedly during training. Its aim is to protect the function without making privacy depend on the number of states at which it is queried. The privacy proof analyzes the noise-space kernel, probabilistic bounds on noise samples, and how privacy guarantees compose across training iterations.

The paper also examines usefulness alongside privacy. It proves approximate optimality when the state space is discrete, providing a utility result under that specific condition. Experiments support the theoretical findings and show improvements over existing approaches. Thus, the continuous-space privacy contribution and the discrete-space optimality result have distinct scopes within the overall method.
neurips-2019-privacy-preserving-q-learni.tldr: Functional noise enables differentially private Q-learning in continuous spaces, with a separate approximate-optimality result for discrete states.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes the Unadjusted Langevin Algorithm, a method for sampling from a probability distribution expressed through a function f. Its focus is mathematical convergence: identifying conditions under which the algorithm has guarantees measured by divergences between probability distributions. The main contribution concerns which assumptions are sufficient to establish those guarantees.

For Kullback-Leibler divergence, the authors assume that the target distribution satisfies a log-Sobolev inequality and that f has a bounded Hessian. The Hessian condition controls second derivatives. Their result does not require f to be convex or impose bounds on higher derivatives. This is significant because the guarantee can apply without the convexity assumption that would otherwise restrict the shapes of functions considered.

The paper also establishes convergence guarantees in Rényi divergence for orders greater than one. Those results assume that the limiting distribution of the algorithm satisfies either a log-Sobolev inequality or a Poincaré inequality. The assumptions therefore attach to different distributions in the two parts of the analysis, and each guarantee depends on its stated functional-inequality conditions.
neurips-2019-rapid-convergence-of-the-un.tldr: ULA receives convergence guarantees under functional-inequality assumptions, including a KL result requiring neither convexity nor higher-derivative bounds.

paragraphs: An empirical risk is the loss computed from observed data, while population risk describes the corresponding average over the underlying distribution. The population landscape can be easier to characterize. This paper asks how to use that simpler landscape to understand a nonconvex empirical loss when the population loss is degenerate, meaning its Hessian can have zero eigenvalues.

The authors first analyze the population risk and then establish a connection to the empirical risk. Their central result gives a correspondence between critical points of the two landscapes without requiring the strongly Morse assumption used in earlier work. Removing that requirement matters because it is not satisfied in the degenerate situations considered here.

The theory is applied to matrix sensing and phase retrieval to demonstrate how population-level analysis can inform the landscape of a loss built from data. The contribution is a way to transfer structural information between these two objectives when flat curvature directions obstruct the earlier assumptions. It supports landscape analysis without requiring a direct characterization of the empirical objective from the outset.
neurips-2019-the-landscape-of-non-convex.tldr: The paper connects empirical and population critical points in degenerate nonconvex problems without the strongly Morse assumption.

paragraphs: Binary neural networks can replace expensive multiplications with simple XNOR operations, making them attractive for hardware with limited resources. Extending this idea to LSTMs is difficult because their computation includes both matrix-vector products and elementwise multiplications. Earlier quantized LSTM approaches described in the abstract retained the latter operations at full precision.

The authors propose converting every multiplication in an LSTM into XNOR operations through stochastic computing. They also introduce a weighted finite-state machine and a synthesis procedure for approximating the nonlinear functions used by LSTMs on stochastic bit streams. This addresses the nonlinear processing needed alongside multiplication, allowing the proposed representation to cover the recurrent computation more completely.

Across the temporal tasks evaluated, the resulting XNOR LSTMs reduce computational complexity by a reported factor of 86 compared with their quantized counterparts. The experiments report better accuracy without sacrificing latency. These are claims about computational complexity, accuracy, and latency in the stated comparisons; together they support the feasibility of implementing more of an LSTM through stochastic logic.
neurips-2019-the-synthesis-of-xnor-recur.tldr: Stochastic logic converts all LSTM multiplications to XNOR operations, with reported 86-fold lower computational complexity and improved accuracy without added latency.

paragraphs: Learning depth and camera motion from unlabeled single-camera video faces two related difficulties. Moving objects violate the static-scene assumption used in geometric image reconstruction. Separately, predictions can use inconsistent scales across frames, preventing individual camera-motion estimates from forming a coherent trajectory over a long video.

The paper introduces a geometry-consistency loss to encourage predictions to share a consistent scale. It also derives a self-discovered mask that handles moving objects and occlusions. These components address consistency and unreliable reconstruction regions within one framework. The authors describe the approach as simpler and more efficient because it avoids the multi-task learning used by recent alternatives.

Evaluation reports state-of-the-art depth-estimation performance on KITTI and globally scale-consistent camera trajectories over long video sequences. Visual-odometry accuracy is competitive with a recent model trained on stereo video. The trajectory result concerns agreement of scale throughout a sequence: it addresses the frame-to-frame inconsistency identified in the paper. The authors present it as, to their knowledge, the first such demonstration using unlabeled monocular training.
neurips-2019-unsupervised-scale-consiste.tldr: Geometry consistency and a learned mask improve monocular depth estimation and enable globally scale-consistent camera trajectories from unlabeled video.

paragraphs: Blind image denoising requires recovering a clean image while also dealing with noise whose properties are not supplied in advance. Real image acquisition can produce complicated noise, making that joint problem difficult. The Variational Denoising Network places noise estimation and image restoration within a single Bayesian framework rather than treating them as unrelated operations.

The method uses deep neural networks to parameterize an approximate posterior conditioned on the noisy input. Both the clean image and noise variances are latent variables to be inferred. Explicit parameterizations make the posterior practical to compute and allow the network to estimate noise automatically for a test image. This formulation gives the learned predictions an interpretation in terms of image content and noise.

The authors combine the efficiency of data-driven neural prediction with the generalization advantages they attribute to generative modeling. The model can estimate and remove complicated noise that is not independent and identically distributed. Comprehensive experiments support its reported superiority in blind denoising, illustrating the value of jointly modeling what the image contains and how its observations are corrupted.
neurips-2019-variational-denoising-netwo.tldr: VDN jointly infers clean images and noise variances through a neural Bayesian model, enabling efficient blind denoising of complicated real-world noise.
